stories.headline: IRAN WAR OIL SHOCK NOW COSTING U.S. HOUSEHOLDS $2,000 A YEAR, MOODY'S FINDS
stories.body: Moody's estimates the eight-month-old U.S.-Iran conflict is costing the average American household roughly $2,000 a year as Brent crude trades near $105.60/bbl and WTI near $92.80/bbl, with 30-year mortgage rates near 7.4%, the highest in nearly three years.
stories.explain: Oil is both a direct CPI component (gasoline, heating) and an input cost that ripples through transportation, plastics, and agriculture, so a sustained Mideast supply shock shows up in headline inflation within weeks, not quarters. That's why the Fed, not just the energy sector, is in the headlines: a cost-push shock forces a choice between tolerating higher inflation or raising rates into weaker growth, since a hike can't add a barrel of oil to the market — it only slows demand enough to offset the price pressure.

stories.headline: FED HIKES FOR FIRST TIME IN THREE YEARS AS 10-YEAR YIELD SITS NEAR A 24-YEAR HIGH
stories.body: The Fed raised its target range in September for the first time since 2023 on war-driven inflation fears, and the 10-year Treasury yield — which touched 5.365% last week, its highest since 2002 — eased about 2 bps to roughly 5.22% today. The Fed's own projections imply one more quarter-point hike by year-end, to about 4.1%.
stories.explain: Yields move opposite to hopes for Fed easing: when the Fed signals it will hold rates higher for longer to fight oil-driven inflation, long-term yields reprice upward because bond buyers demand more compensation for holding duration risk in a higher-rate world. That 24-year-high 10-year yield is also the direct channel pushing 30-year mortgage rates toward 7.4%, since fixed mortgages are priced off the 10-year plus a spread.

stories.headline: OIL EASES OFF MULTI-MONTH HIGHS ON RUSSIAN DIESEL RELIEF, BUT GOLDMAN SEES MORE UPSIDE RISK
stories.body: Brent slipped about 1% to $105.60/bbl and WTI eased to $92.80/bbl today as extra Russian diesel supply eased some tightness, even as Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90/bbl from $85, calling renewed Iran-war escalation a 'significant upside risk.'
stories.explain: Goldman's $90 forecast sits below today's spot price, which signals the market is still pricing a meaningful geopolitical risk premium into oil beyond what fundamentals alone justify. If a ceasefire materializes, that premium could unwind quickly and pull inflation expectations, Treasury yields, and the Fed's hiking path down with it.

stories.headline: NASDAQ-100 SLIDES TOWARD CORRECTION AS CHIP AND MEMORY STOCKS SELL OFF FOR A FIFTH STRAIGHT SESSION
stories.body: The Nasdaq-100 fell to roughly 30,457 (-0.59%) as the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped for a fifth consecutive session, with Micron down 3.6% and Applied Materials off nearly 7%. The S&P 500 was essentially flat at 7,805.45 (-0.02%) and the Dow fell 180 points (-0.35%).
stories.explain: Chip and memory names carry outsized weight in the Nasdaq-100 after years of AI-driven gains, so a sector-specific unwind — here tied to memory-pricing and capex-sentiment worries — can drag the whole index toward correction territory (a 10%+ pullback from highs) even while the broader, more diversified S&P 500 barely moves.

stories.headline: BIG BANKS TOP ESTIMATES BUT SHARES WHIPSAW AS MIDEAST RISK CLOUDS THE OUTLOOK
stories.body: Major banks reporting this week, including Goldman Sachs, beat profit expectations for the quarter, but shares flipped between gains and losses intraday as investors weighed strong trading and lending results against the inflation and growth risks from the Iran war and higher-for-longer rates.
stories.explain: Higher rates are a double-edged sword for banks: net interest margins widen as banks earn more on loans funded by cheaper deposits, which flattered this quarter's results, but a rate shock driven by an external supply crisis also raises credit risk and the odds of a growth slowdown, so the market is still deciding whether this quarter's beat is sustainable or a last good print before the cycle turns.

stories.headline: FLORIDA TOPS ESPN'S WAY-TOO-EARLY PRESEASON TOP 25 AS MICHIGAN AND UCONN OPEN NEW ERAS
stories.body: With tip-off three weeks away (Nov. 2), ESPN's preseason Top 25 projects Florida at No. 1, while KenPom's model favors Duke. Reigning champion Michigan and runner-up UConn both enter the season under heavy roster turnover, and the AP's official preseason poll has not yet been released.

stories.headline: LAKERS FRANCHISE SALE CLOSES AT A RECORD $12 BILLION AMID A ROCKY START TO THE SEASON
stories.body: ESPN reports the Lakers' ownership sale has closed at a record $12 billion valuation for an NBA franchise, even as the team opened the preseason without Luka Doncic, whom coach JJ Redick says is out indefinitely, and with LeBron James reportedly managing chronic arthritis entering the year.

stories.headline: 49ERS STAY UNBEATEN AT 5-0, RALLYING PAST SEAHAWKS 32-29 ON TWO LATE PURDY DRIVES
stories.body: Brock Purdy led two fourth-quarter scoring drives as San Francisco overcame a 26-21 deficit to beat Seattle 32-29 at Lumen Field on Sunday, improving to 5-0 and dropping the Seahawks to 3-2 in a chippy game with three Seattle turnovers.

stories.headline: GEORGIA RISES TO NO. 1 IN LATEST AP TOP 25 AS TEXAS AND OREGON TUMBLE
stories.body: Georgia (6-0) moved to No. 1 with 66 first-place votes in this week's AP poll, followed by Notre Dame, Miami, Ohio State, and Indiana. Texas dropped to No. 7 after a loss, and Oregon fell out of the rankings entirely despite drawing votes.

deepDive.title: Supply Shocks vs. the Fed: Why an Oil War Forces a Hawkish Pivot
content: Today's brief has three numbers that all trace back to one cause: oil near $105.60 Brent and $92.80 WTI, a 10-year Treasury yield sitting near a 24-year high at 5.22%, and a Fed that just hiked for the first time in three years. The common thread is the eight-month-old U.S.-Iran conflict, which Moody's now estimates costs the average American household about $2,000 a year. That is an unusual combination — a central bank tightening policy while a war, not an overheating economy, is doing most of the damage — and it is exactly the kind of setup that tests whether monetary policy is built to handle a supply shock at all.

The mechanism starts with oil's dual role in the price level. It is a direct line item in CPI through gasoline and home heating, so a Brent move from the mid-$70s to the $100s shows up in headline inflation within a single reporting cycle. But oil is also an input cost for trucking, plastics, fertilizer, and air travel, so the effect compounds over the following months as businesses pass through higher shipping and production costs. A central bank facing this has no tool that adds a barrel of oil to the market. All it can do is raise the cost of borrowing enough that consumers and businesses pull back on everything else, which cools demand until it roughly offsets the energy-driven price pressure — a blunt, recessionary way to fight an inflation problem that didn't originate in excess demand to begin with.

This is precisely the dilemma that defined the 1973-74 oil embargo, when OPEC's price shock hit a Fed that chose to look through it rather than tighten aggressively, on the theory that a supply shock wasn't a monetary problem. Inflation expectations de-anchored instead, and the 1970s ended in stagflation that took Paul Volcker's brutal rate hikes years later to unwind. Today's Fed is explicitly trying not to repeat that mistake: hiking into a war-driven shock is a bet that acting early on expectations is cheaper than waiting and having to act later with much higher rates. The market is pricing that bet directly — Goldman's $90 December Brent forecast sits below today's spot price precisely because it assumes some of today's war premium eventually fades.

For the here and now, that framework explains why a 24-year-high 10-year yield is squeezing markets on two fronts at once. It is pushing 30-year mortgage rates toward 7.4%, since fixed mortgages price directly off the 10-year plus a spread, and it is the discount-rate pressure behind the Nasdaq-100's slide toward correction, since higher-duration growth and chip stocks get hit hardest when the rate used to discount their future earnings rises. The next data point to watch isn't a jobs report — it's any Iran ceasefire headline, because that's the one shock that could pull oil, yields, and the Fed's remaining rate-hike path back down together, faster than any single piece of economic data.
